title: Metrics, Logs & Traces: Prometheus, Grafana & ELK
summary: Build full observability: Prometheus pull model and PromQL, Grafana RED dashboards, the EFK logging pipeline, the Azure Monitor mapping, and the sampling-and-aggregation architecture that survives millions of transactions per second.
objectives: Explain the Prometheus pull model and choose Counter, Gauge, and Histogram correctly
Write PromQL for rates, error ratios, and latency quantiles, and design recording rules
Build Grafana dashboards using the RED and USE methods with variables and deploy annotations
Operate the EFK pipeline and triage error spikes via filter-aggregate-pivot
Design observability for millions of txns/sec using cardinality discipline, sampling, and tiered retention

notes.title: Prometheus: The Pull Model and Metric Types
notes.body: Prometheus monitors by scraping: it pulls metrics from HTTP endpoints (usually /metrics) on a fixed interval, storing timestamped samples in its time-series database. Pull inverts the usual push assumption and buys you three things: targets can die without losing the monitoring path's knowledge of them (failed scrapes are themselves a signal via the 'up' metric), service discovery (Kubernetes, EC2, DNS) keeps the target list fresh automatically, and exporters are dumb text endpoints — any app can expose metrics with a client library. Four metric types: Counter (monotonically increasing: http_requests_total), Gauge (goes up and down: memory usage, queue depth), Histogram (observations bucketed for latency quantiles), Summary (precomputed quantiles, less flexible). Worked example: your API exposes http_requests_total{method,code} and http_request_duration_seconds_bucket. Which type answers 'requests per second'? Solution: a Counter — rate(http_requests_total[5m]). Which answers 'current queue depth'? A Gauge — read directly. Which answers 'p99 latency'? The Histogram — histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])). The classic mistake is rate() on a Gauge (meaningless — gauges are not cumulative) or averaging a Counter directly (use rate first).

notes.title: PromQL Basics: rate, increase, and histogram_quantile
notes.body: PromQL is Prometheus's query language; a handful of functions covers most operational questions. rate(v range-vector[5m]) gives per-second average increase — the standard way to read counters. increase() gives the total increase over the window. sum by (label) aggregates: sum by (service) (rate(http_requests_total[5m])). avg_over_time, max_over_time smooth gauges. histogram_quantile(0.99, ...) computes the p99 from histogram buckets. Alert expressions combine these with thresholds: rate(http_requests_total{code=~'5..'}[5m]) / rate(http_requests_total[5m]) > 0.05 fires when the 5xx ratio exceeds 5%. Worked example: 'Is checkout slower than yesterday?' Solution: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{route='/checkout'}[5m]))) and compare against the same query with a 24h offset modifier. Second: 'Which pod is OOMKilled most?' — increase(kube_pod_container_status_terminated_reason{reason='OOMKilled'}[1h]) sorted by pod. The trap: rate() needs at least two samples in the window — on a 30s scrape interval, a [1m] window is fragile; use [5m] for stability. And remember counters reset on restart — rate() handles resets, but naive subtraction does not.

notes.title: Grafana: Dashboards That Answer Questions
notes.body: Grafana turns Prometheus (and other sources) into dashboards, but a dashboard is only as good as the questions it answers. Design by the RED method per service — Rate (requests/sec), Errors (error ratio), Duration (latency quantiles) — plus the USE method per resource — Utilization, Saturation, Errors. One row per service with its RED panels; one row per dependency (database, queue) with USE panels. Variables make dashboards reusable: a $namespace or $service dropdown templating every query. Annotations mark deploys so you can correlate a latency spike with the release that caused it. Worked example: build the checkout dashboard. Panels: (1) rate of checkouts: sum(rate(checkout_completed_total[5m])); (2) error ratio: 5xx rate / total rate with a 1% alert threshold line; (3) p50/p95/p99 latency via histogram_quantile; (4) saturation: container CPU throttling rate and memory working set vs limit. Solution review: each panel maps to RED; variables let the same dashboard serve every service; the deploy annotation answers 'what changed?' in one glance. The anti-pattern is the wall of 40 graphs nobody reads — if a panel has never triggered a decision, delete it. Dashboards are operational tools, not art.

notes.title: Centralized Logging: The EFK Pipeline
notes.body: Metrics tell you something is wrong; logs tell you why. The EFK stack — Elasticsearch, Fluent Bit/Fluentd, Kibana (or OpenSearch equivalents) — centralizes logs because containers are ephemeral: when a pod dies, its local logs die with it. The pipeline: application writes structured JSON logs to stdout; the node agent (Fluent Bit as a DaemonSet) tails container logs, parses and enriches them (adds pod, namespace, node labels), and ships to Elasticsearch; Kibana queries and visualizes. Structured logging is the prerequisite — log {timestamp, level, service, trace_id, message, fields} as JSON, never free text, so every field is filterable. Worked example: checkout errors spike; find the cause. Solution: in Kibana, filter level=error AND service=checkout over the spike window, aggregate by fields.error_code — one code dominates; expand a sample document, copy its trace_id, pivot to the trace view to see the failing downstream call. The cost trap is log volume: debug logging in production at millions of transactions per second will bankrupt your Elasticsearch cluster. Set levels per environment (info in prod, debug in dev), sample high-volume access logs, and set index retention (hot 7 days, warm 30, delete after 90) before the disk fills.

notes.title: Azure Monitor: The Native Mapping
notes.body: On Azure, the native observability stack is Azure Monitor: metrics flow into Metrics Explorer, logs into Log Analytics workspaces queried with KQL, and Application Insights provides APM (distributed traces, dependency maps) for applications. Container Insights onboards AKS clusters to collect Prometheus metrics and container logs without running your own stack. The mapping to this module: Prometheus ~ Azure Monitor metrics, Grafana ~ Metrics Explorer/dashboards (or Grafana with the Azure data source), EFK ~ Log Analytics + KQL, Alertmanager ~ Azure Monitor alert rules with action groups. Worked example: replicate the checkout RED dashboard natively. Solution: Container Insights collects the Prometheus endpoints; a Log Analytics query (KQL) aggregates: ContainerLog | where LogEntry contains 'ERROR' | summarize count() by bin(TimeGenerated, 5m); an alert rule fires an action group (email + webhook + PagerDuty) when the 5xx ratio crosses the SLO threshold. The decision framework: run Prometheus/Grafana/EFK yourself for portability and PromQL familiarity across clouds (the multicloud answer from M44), or adopt Azure Monitor for zero-operational-overhead on Azure with KQL as the query skill. Most enterprises end up hybrid: Prometheus for K8s metrics, Azure Monitor for platform/audit logs.

notes.title: Observability at Millions of Transactions per Second
notes.body: The panel asks how you do logging and monitoring at millions of transactions per second — the answer is sampling, aggregation, and cardinality discipline, because naive 'log everything, label everything' collapses. Metrics: keep label cardinality bounded — a label with a million distinct values (like user_id or request_id) creates a million time series and will OOM your Prometheus; aggregate at the edge and drop high-cardinality labels via relabeling. Use recording rules to precompute expensive queries (the 5xx ratio per service computed once, read by every dashboard). Logs: sample aggressively (1% of success logs, 100% of errors), structure everything, and ship to a tiered store. Traces: head-based sampling at low rates plus tail-based sampling that keeps all error traces — you need the failures, not the successes. Worked example: checkout does 2M txns/sec; the team wants per-request logs and per-user latency metrics. Solution: per-user latency as a metric is rejected (cardinality explosion); instead histogram by route with bounded labels, recording rules for the SLO ratios, 1% sampled success logs + 100% error logs, and tail-sampled traces keeping errors. The panel one-liner: 'At scale, observability is a sampling and aggregation architecture, not a collection architecture.'

cards.front: Prometheus pull vs push: what does a failed scrape tell you?
cards.back: The 'up' metric goes to 0 — target death is itself a signal; pull means the monitor knows about outages rather than waiting for pushes that never come

cards.front: Counter vs Gauge vs Histogram (one use each)
cards.back: Counter: requests total (rate it). Gauge: queue depth (read directly). Histogram: latency buckets (histogram_quantile for p99)

cards.front: PromQL: requests per second from http_requests_total
cards.back: rate(http_requests_total[5m]) — or sum by (service) (rate(...)) to aggregate

cards.front: PromQL: p99 latency from a histogram
Why is rate() on a Gauge wrong?
cards.back: Gauges are not cumulative — rate assumes ever-increasing counters and handles resets; on a gauge it produces nonsense
RED per service: Rate, Errors, Duration. USE per resource: Utilization, Saturation, Errors

cards.front: Why structured JSON logs are a prerequisite
cards.back: Every field becomes filterable/aggregatable; free-text logs cannot be pivoted by error_code or trace_id during an incident

cards.front: Azure Monitor mapping: Prometheus / Grafana / EFK / Alertmanager
cards.back: Metrics ~ Monitor metrics; dashboards ~ Metrics Explorer (or Grafana w/ Azure source); logs ~ Log Analytics + KQL; alerts ~ alert rules + action groups

cards.front: Cardinality discipline: why not label metrics by user_id?
cards.back: Each distinct label value creates a time series — a million users = a million series = Prometheus OOM. Aggregate at the edge; drop high-cardinality labels

quiz.q: Which PromQL query gives per-service requests per second?
quiz.explain: rate() converts the counter to per-second; sum by (service) aggregates across instances. Bare counters and avg() are meaningless for rates.

quiz.q: You need p99 checkout latency. Which is correct?
quiz.explain: Quantiles come from histogram buckets via histogram_quantile; avg/max of raw observations are not available from aggregated exposition and max is not p99.

quiz.q: A dashboard panel shows rate(queue_depth[5m]). What is wrong?
choices: queue_depth is a Gauge — rate() on a gauge is meaningless; read it directly
quiz.explain: rate() assumes a cumulative counter and corrects for resets; applied to a gauge it fabricates values. Gauges are read as-is or smoothed with avg_over_time.

quiz.q: Checkout errors spike. Fastest EFK triage path?
choices: Kibana: filter level=error AND service=checkout over the window, aggregate by error_code, pivot on trace_id
Increase log verbosity to debug everywhere
quiz.explain: Structured logs make this a three-step pivot: filter, aggregate, trace. SSH-ing into ephemeral pods or enabling debug at scale makes things worse.

quiz.q: At 2M txns/sec, the team wants a per-user-id latency metric. Your response?
choices: Reject: cardinality explosion — a million label values means a million time series; use bounded labels + histograms + recording rules
quiz.explain: High-cardinality labels OOM Prometheus. Latency by route with histograms answers the operational question without per-user series.

quiz.q: Which sampling strategy keeps all error traces at high throughput?
choices: Head-based sampling at low rates plus tail-based sampling that retains error traces
quiz.explain: Tail-based sampling decides after seeing the outcome, so it can keep 100% of failures while dropping the bulk of successes.

quiz.q: In Azure-native terms, what replaces Alertmanager?
choices: Azure Monitor alert rules with action groups
quiz.explain: Alert rules evaluate the signal (metric/log query) and action groups route the notification — the same separation Alertmanager provides.

quiz.q: A recording rule precomputes the per-service 5xx ratio. Why?
choices: Expensive queries run once at scrape time instead of on every dashboard load and alert evaluation
quiz.explain: Recording rules trade a little storage for a lot of query-time savings — critical when many dashboards and alerts share the same ratio.

quiz.q: Debug logging is enabled in production at high throughput and the logging bill explodes. What are the two fixes?
choices: Per-environment log levels (info in prod) plus sampling of high-volume success logs, with tiered retention
quiz.explain: Volume control happens at the source (levels, sampling) and at the store (hot/warm/delete retention tiers). Scaling the store without fixing the source just moves the bill.

items.explain: rate then aggregate — the most-written query in operations.
Regex matcher on code; ratio of rates, not rate of ratios.
Buckets, not raw observations — the _bucket suffix matters.

items.prompt: Why [5m] and not [1m] with a 30s scrape interval?
items.answer: [1m] holds ~2 samples — fragile; [5m] smooths missed scrapes and restarts.
items.explain: rate needs multiple samples; short windows on sparse scrapes lie.

items.prompt: Counter vs Gauge: which gets rate(), which is read directly?
items.answer: Counters get rate(); gauges are read directly (or avg_over_time).
items.explain: Say the rule and the reason: rate assumes cumulative + resets.

items.prompt: Which pod is being OOMKilled most in the last hour? Write it.
items.explain: increase over the window, grouped by pod — leads straight to the memory-limit fix.

items.prompt: What does the 'up' metric tell you, and why does pull make it possible?
items.answer: up==0 means the scrape failed (target down). Pull makes target death a first-class signal.
items.explain: Push systems learn about death by absence; pull learns by failed attempt.

items.answer: RED per service: Rate, Errors, Duration. USE per resource: Utilization, Saturation, Errors.
items.explain: RED for services, USE for resources — dashboard design in two acronyms.

items.prompt: EFK pipeline: name the four stages.
items.answer: Structured stdout logs -> Fluent Bit DaemonSet tail/enrich -> Elasticsearch store -> Kibana query.
items.explain: Ephemeral pods make centralization mandatory, not optional.

items.prompt: Checkout errors spike. Your 3-step Kibana triage?
items.answer: Filter level=error+service over window; aggregate by error_code; pivot on trace_id.
items.explain: Filter, aggregate, pivot — say it as the muscle-memory sequence.

items.prompt: Why reject a per-user_id latency metric at 2M txns/sec?
items.answer: Cardinality explosion: a million label values = a million series = Prometheus OOM.
items.explain: Bounded labels + histograms + recording rules instead.

items.prompt: Log strategy at 2M txns/sec: successes vs errors?
items.answer: Sample successes aggressively (e.g. 1%); keep 100% of errors; structured JSON always.
items.explain: You need the failures, not the successes — volume control at the source.

items.prompt: Map to Azure native: Prometheus, Grafana, EFK, Alertmanager.
items.answer: Monitor metrics, Metrics Explorer/dashboards, Log Analytics+KQL, alert rules + action groups.
items.explain: Know both stacks; justify the choice (portability vs zero-ops).

items.prompt: Panel: 'observability at millions of txns/sec' — your one-liner?
items.answer: 'At scale, observability is a sampling and aggregation architecture: bounded cardinality, recording rules, sampled logs, tail-sampled traces.'
items.explain: Then unpack each of the four on demand — the one-liner opens, the details close.

handsOnLab.title: Lab: Prometheus + Grafana + EFK on a local stack
handsOnLab.brief: You will run Prometheus, Grafana, and an EFK pipeline with Docker Compose, instrument a sample Python API with RED metrics and structured logs, build the checkout-style dashboard, and practice the error-spike triage end to end.
steps: Create the lab dir and docker-compose.yml with Prometheus (prom/prometheus), Grafana (grafana/grafana), Elasticsearch (single-node), Fluent Bit, and Kibana. Pin image tags.
Write prometheus.yml scraping your sample API at api:8000/metrics every 15s plus itself; add a recording rule file computing job:5xx_ratio:rate5m.

Write the sample API (Python + prometheus_client): expose http_requests_total (Counter), http_request_duration_seconds (Histogram), queue_depth (Gauge); log structured JSON to stdout with trace_id per request.
Start the stack: docker-compose up -d; verify Prometheus targets at localhost:9090/targets (all UP) and Grafana at localhost:3000.
In Prometheus, run sum by (route) (rate(http_requests_total[5m])) and the p99 histogram_quantile query; confirm numbers move when you curl the API in a loop.
Generate an error spike: hit a /fail endpoint 200 times; watch the 5xx ratio recording rule climb in Prometheus.
Build the Grafana dashboard: one row, four panels — request rate, error ratio (with 1% threshold line), p50/p95/p99 latency, queue depth gauge. Add a $route variable.
Configure Fluent Bit to tail the API container logs, parse JSON, and ship to Elasticsearch; verify documents in Kibana under an index pattern.
In Kibana, filter level=error over the spike window, aggregate by error_code, and pivot on a trace_id — write down the three steps and what each revealed.
Add a Prometheus alert rule: 5xx ratio > 5% for 5m; trigger it with the /fail loop and confirm the alert fires in the Prometheus UI.
Break cardinality deliberately: add a user_id label to a counter, generate traffic, and watch active series explode (Prometheus status page) — then remove the label and note the lesson.
Document the scale plan: for 2M txns/sec, write which labels you would keep/drop, your sampling rates, and your retention tiers. Tear down with docker-compose down -v.
handsOnLab.deliverable: A running-then-removed local observability stack, a RED Grafana dashboard, a written Kibana triage walkthrough, and a one-page 'observability at 2M txns/sec' scale plan.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Dashboard panels answer rate/errors/duration; the alert fires on the induced spike; Kibana triage finds the error_code; the scale plan names kept/dropped labels with reasons.

mockTask.q: Panel: 'How do you do logging and monitoring at millions of transactions per second?' What is the core of a strong answer?
choices: Log every request with full detail and alert on all of it
Sampling and aggregation architecture: bounded label cardinality, recording rules, sampled success logs with 100% of errors, tail-sampled traces keeping failures
Disable monitoring in production for performance
mockTask.explain: Scale breaks naive collection: unbounded labels OOM Prometheus, full logging bankrupts storage. The strong answer names the four controls (cardinality, recording rules, log sampling, trace sampling) and the one-liner: observability at scale is a sampling and aggregation architecture.
